terroir.climate: Continental with a Mediterranean cast: cold winters that can bring snow, warm summers and a long, dry ripening season running into October. Mount Vermio to the west takes the worst of the weather, the slopes face east and south-east into the morning sun, and the Thermaic Gulf, some way east, blunts the extremes. Rainfall is higher than on the islands and spring can be wet, so downy mildew is the standing threat and hail the occasional one. Xinomavro ripens late and needs every week of that autumn.
terroir.soils: A patchwork rather than one soil. The old core is calcareous clay-loam over limestone bedrock, which gives the firmest and longest-lived wines; the lower, eastern ground around Trilofos is sandier and lighter and gives softer Xinomavro that drinks sooner; and bands of schist and gravel show on the higher and western ground. Drainage is good almost everywhere, which matters for a rot-prone grape in a district with real rain.
terroir.topography: The vineyards lie on the eastern and south-eastern foothills of Mount Vermio in a belt roughly between 150 and 350 metres above sea level, with a few sites higher, around the town of Naoussa and a ring of villages. Altitude and aspect change the wine: the higher, cooler sites to the north and west ripen later and keep more acid and perfume, while the lower, warmer ground to the east and south gives fuller fruit and rounder tannin.
terroir.water: The Arapitsa, a mountain stream that drops through the town of Naoussa, once drove its textile mills and still marks the heart of the district; otherwise the vines live on Vermio's rain and snowmelt. The Aliakmonas, the longest river wholly in Greece, passes well to the south on its way to the Thermaic Gulf, and the gulf's breath is a distant moderating influence rather than a daily one.

traps: Naoussa is red only: a Xinomavro rosé or sparkling wine from the same slopes is PGI Imathia or Macedonia, and Amyndeon is the appellation that allows them.
Pale colour is the grape, not a fault or a sign of a thin wine; Xinomavro's brick rim arrives early and says nothing about age or extraction.
Xinomavro is compared with Nebbiolo for structure and aroma, but Naoussa sits lower and warmer than Barolo and its tomato and olive note is its own; the comparison is not a claim of relation.
Rapsani uses Xinomavro too but blends it with Krassato and Stavroto; Goumenissa blends it with Negoska; only Naoussa and Amyndeon use it alone.
Macedonia here is the Greek region around Thessaloniki, not the neighbouring country to the north.
The Boutari firm and Kir-Yianni share a family origin but are separate companies with separate wines.
Reserve and Grande Reserve are national ageing terms, not Naoussa's own classification; the appellation ranks no vineyard.

wines.note: Pale garnet turning to brick within a few years, with sour cherry, sun-dried tomato, black olive, dried rose and sweet spice, searing acidity and a firm grip. Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, decant a young bottle, and pour it with roast lamb, game birds, mushrooms or a tomato-rich braise.

Longer in cask and bottle before release: the tannin starts to soften and leather, tobacco and dried fig join the tomato and olive. The classic style of the old houses, and a wine for slow-cooked meat and aged cheese.

Four years' ageing at least, divided between cask and bottle, released tawny-edged with dried flowers, tar, dried tomato and a long savoury finish; the Greek bottle most often set beside an old Barolo at a blind tasting.

The modern school's wine: a short maceration, some whole bunches and little or no new oak give bright red cherry, tomato skin and rose over a lighter frame. Serve a touch cooler, around 15 degrees, with charcuterie, grilled vegetables or a lamb burger.

Rosé and sparkling Xinomavro and the Xinomavro blends with Merlot or Syrah leave the appellation and go out as PGI Imathia or PGI Macedonia; the rosé is pale, strawberry-scented and sharp, and a good aperitif.

exam: Agiorgitiko: St George's grape, Greece's most planted red, 100% of Nemea, deep colour, soft tannin, plum and spice.
The place: Corinthia, north-eastern Peloponnese, south-west of Corinth; Greece's largest red appellation; 1971.
The three bands: floor on red clay, slopes with Koutsi, plateau at Asprokambos, and how altitude changes the wine.
What is and is not Nemea: dry and sweet red yes; rosé, white and blends no, they are PGI Peloponnese or Corinth.
The ageing terms Reserve and Grande Reserve, shared with every Greek PDO red, four years at least for Grande Reserve.
Hercules and the Nemean lion, the Nemean Games at Ancient Nemea, and the old name blood of Hercules.
Service: 15 to 17 degrees, the easiest Greek red with lamb, moussaka and tomato dishes; Reserve with roast meat.

grapes.name: Agiorgitiko
grapes.styles: St George's grape, the only grape of the appellation and Greece's most planted red: deep purple, plum, sour cherry, sweet spice and a soft, rounded tannin; from rosé and light reds to oak-aged, long-lived wine, and sweet wine from dried grapes.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The partner in the district's famous regional blends, where it stiffens Agiorgitiko's soft frame; never part of a wine labelled Nemea.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Grown on the slopes for PGI Peloponnese varietals and blends alongside Agiorgitiko.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: A warm-climate red the estates grow for regional wine, blended with or sold beside Agiorgitiko under the PGI.

grapes.name: Roditis
grapes.styles: The pink-skinned white of the district's regional whites, simple and fresh, outside the appellation.

grapes.name: Malagousia
grapes.styles: The revived aromatic white, planted by Nemea estates for peach-scented PGI whites to pour beside the red.

law.classification: Nemea is a protected designation of origin from the first Greek decrees of 1971, covering a delimited zone of villages in the Corinthia regional unit of the north-eastern Peloponnese, the largest red appellation in Greece by area. The grape is Agiorgitiko alone. The appellation covers red wine only: dry, semi-sweet and sweet, the sweet made from dried grapes or fortified, though sweet Nemea is rare; rosé, white and any blend with another variety are sold as PGI Peloponnese or PGI Corinth. The national Reserve and Grande Reserve ageing terms apply, four years at least for Grande Reserve. The three altitude bands, floor, slopes and plateau, are a grower's and a sommelier's convention, not a legal sub-zoning, and no vineyard or village is officially ranked, though village and vineyard names appear on labels at the producer's choice.
labels: St George's grape, the only grape of Nemea; it may stand with the appellation name
the national ageing terms, Epilegmenos and Eidika Epilegmenos
sweet, semi-sweet: the rare sweet reds the appellation allows
village names a producer may print beside Nemea; they are addresses, not crus
tiers: Nemea PDO dry red
Dry red from 100% Agiorgitiko grown within the delimited villages of Corinthia; the largest red appellation in Greece.
Nemea PDO sweet red
The traditional sweet red from sun-dried or overripe Agiorgitiko, naturally sweet or fortified, with a semi-sweet red beside it: the heritage styles of the valley floor, rarely seen.
Nemea Reserve
The national Reserve term for PDO reds, Epilegmenos: extended ageing in oak and bottle before release.
Nemea Grande Reserve
The national Grande Reserve term, Eidika Epilegmenos: four years' ageing at least, divided between oak and bottle.
PGI Peloponnese and PGI Corinth
The regional wines of the same vineyards: Agiorgitiko rosé, blends with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot or Syrah, and the whites.

made.viticulture: Agiorgitiko is vigorous and productive and will crop heavily if allowed, and its bunches are compact enough to rot in a wet September, so the work of the year is restraint and timing. Most vineyards are on wires with vertical shoot positioning and a leaf-plucked fruit zone to keep air moving through the bunches; older plots are bush vines. Yields are held down by pruning and a green harvest, because an overloaded vine gives a pale, dilute wine that still tastes sweet. Virus has been a long-standing problem in the district's old plant material and the estates have replanted with cleaner vines. Harvest runs from early September on the valley floor to early October on the plateau, by hand on the slopes; hail in summer and rain at picking are the hazards, and drought on the lower ground in a hot year. The great choice is altitude: the floor for sweet wine and easy reds, the slopes for the serious dry wine, the plateau for freshness and rosé.
made.winemaking: Agiorgitiko has colour and fruit to spare and tannin that is soft by nature, so the winemaker's task is structure rather than restraint. The dry wine is destemmed and fermented in stainless steel with a maceration of one to three weeks, longer on the slopes for the Reserve wines; malolactic follows in tank or barrel. Oak is used widely, French barriques and larger casks, new oak on the top wines, with twelve months common and the national terms for Reserve and Grande Reserve. Blends with Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot are assembled after ageing and leave the appellation as regional wine, as do the rosé, made by short skin contact or direct pressing, and the whites. The sweet wine is made from sun-dried or overripe Agiorgitiko, fermented to a natural sweetness or fortified, and aged in cask. The modern estates have moved from heavy extraction and new oak towards fresher, earlier-picked wines that show the villages.

places.name: The valley floor
places.note: The lowest band, about 250 to 400 metres around Nemea town and Ancient Nemea, on red clay: the warmest ground, early harvests, plush easy reds and the home of the sweet wine.

places.name: Nemea
places.note: The market town of the appellation, in the valley at the foot of the slopes, with the growers' cooperative and several of the district's longest-established houses nearby.

places.name: Ancient Nemea (Archaia Nemea)
places.note: The sanctuary of Zeus and the stadium of the Nemean Games, a short way from the town, where the lion of Hercules's first labour was said to live; several estates farm the vineyards around the ruins.

places.name: Archaies Kleones
places.note: Ancient Kleonai, a village on the road towards Corinth at the edge of the zone, with vineyards on the valley's clay and the slopes above it and the base of one well-known family house.

places.name: The slopes
places.note: The middle band, roughly 400 to 650 metres, on clay over limestone: the heart of dry Nemea, where the best estates have their vineyards and where Reserve and Grande Reserve are made.

places.name: Koutsi
places.note: The most famous hillside of Nemea, south-west of the town around 500 to 600 metres on clay-limestone: the address of several leading estates and the village most often printed on a top Nemea.

places.name: Gymno
places.note: A village of the slopes at the upper edge of the middle band, with cooler sites that give structured, fresher Agiorgitiko.

places.name: Psari
places.note: A high village of the upper slopes on stony limestone, with old vines and some of the latest harvests of the middle band.

places.name: Leontio
places.note: A village of the slopes with cooler, breezier sites, whose vineyards several estates use for fresher reds.

places.name: Kastraki
places.note: Little castle: a hillside village of the zone with clay-limestone vineyards supplying several Nemea houses.

places.name: The plateau
places.note: The high band, about 650 to 900 metres, on sandy limestone: the coolest ground, late harvests, bright acid, and fruit once used mainly for rosé and light red that the best growers now make into fine structured Nemea.

places.name: Asprokambos
places.note: White plain: the high plateau in the south-west of the zone around 800 metres, the coolest and latest site, named on labels for fresh, structured Agiorgitiko.

places.name: Petri
places.note: A high village of the upper band on the plateau's limestone, with old plantings of the upper zone.

places.name: Mount Kyllini
places.note: The mountain west of the zone, over 2,300 metres, the ancient Cyllene where Hermes was said to be born; its bulk shelters the upper vineyards and feeds the cool air that settles on the plateau at night.

producers.name: Gaia Wines
producers.why: Founded in 1994 with vineyards at Koutsi; its Gaia Estate Agiorgitiko is the reference for structured, age-worthy Nemea, and the house also makes Santorini, so one name links the exam's two Greek answers.

producers.name: Skouras
producers.why: A house near Argos with vineyards in Nemea, whose Grande Cuvée Nemea and whose Megas Oenos, an Agiorgitiko and Cabernet Sauvignon blend, set the modern style for the Peloponnese from the late 1980s.

producers.name: Papaioannou
producers.why: A family estate at Ancient Nemea, among the first in the district to bottle estate wine in the 1980s and a benchmark for traditional, cask-aged Nemea and old-vine Agiorgitiko.

producers.name: Palivou
producers.why: An estate at Ancient Nemea with a broad range from fresh Agiorgitiko to Reserve, a sound study of the appellation end to end.

producers.name: Semeli
producers.why: A large modern estate at Koutsi, above the valley, whose Nemea Reserve and Grande Reserve show the slopes' structure; also known for Mantinia whites.

producers.name: Driopi
producers.why: The Nemea estate of a leading Mantinia house, at Koutsi, whose Driopi Classic and Reserve are among the most polished expressions of the slopes.

producers.name: Lafkiotis
producers.why: A family house at Ancient Kleones making straightforward Nemea in volume, the sort of bottle that teaches the appellation at a tavern price.

producers.name: The Nemea Wine Cooperative
producers.why: The growers' cooperative in the town, which handles a large share of the district's grapes and bottles honest Nemea under its own labels.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean: hot, dry summers, mild wet winters and a long sunny autumn, with altitude doing the work of latitude. The valley floor around Nemea town bakes and ripens Agiorgitiko early and fully; the hillside villages at 400 to 650 metres have cooler nights and keep acid; and the plateau at 650 to 900 metres is cool enough to make rosé and fresh red and to ripen late. Breezes from the Gulf of Corinth reach down the valleys, hail is the summer hazard and autumn rain on a thin-skinned grape the harvest one.
terroir.soils: Red clay on the valley floor, iron-rich and fertile, giving the fleshy, generous wines and the sweet tradition; clay over limestone and marl on the slopes, where drainage improves and the tannin tightens; sandier and stonier limestone ground on the high plateau. Water-holding clay below and free-draining limestone above is the simplest way to explain why altitude and soil pull in the same direction here.
terroir.topography: A basin of valleys and rolling hills between the Corinthian coast to the north and the plain of Argos to the south, with Mount Kyllini rising to the west. The vineyards lie between roughly 250 and 900 metres: the floor around Nemea town and Ancient Nemea, the slopes of Koutsi, Gymno, Psari, Leontio and Kastraki, and the plateau of Asprokambos and Petri at the top. The three bands are growers' convention, not law, but the exam uses them.
terroir.water: The Nemea stream drains the basin north to the Gulf of Corinth, whose breezes reach the lower vineyards; otherwise the district is dry through the summer and relies on the clay's reserves below and the cool nights above.

traps: Nemea is in the Peloponnese, not Macedonia; Naoussa is the northern red. Agiorgitiko and Xinomavro are the two great Greek reds and the exam loves to swap their homes.
Nemea rosé does not exist as an appellation wine; an Agiorgitiko rosé is PGI Peloponnese or PGI Corinth.
The three altitude bands are convention, not law: no Nemea label is legally a floor, slope or plateau wine.
Agiorgitiko's soft tannin is varietal; a structured Nemea gets its grip from altitude, yield and oak, not from the grape's nature.
Nemea permits a sweet red, from dried grapes or fortified; it is a Nemea tradition, not a Naoussa one, and it is rare beside the dry wine.
Megas Oenos and the other famous Agiorgitiko and Cabernet blends are not Nemea, whatever the producer's fame; they are regional wines.
Olympia and the Olympic Games are in the western Peloponnese; the Nemean Games were at Ancient Nemea, one of the four Panhellenic games.

wines.note: Deep purple to ruby, with plum, black cherry, sour cherry, sweet spice and a floral note, medium acid and a soft, velvety tannin; unoaked or lightly oaked and ready young. Serve at 15 to 17 degrees with grilled lamb, pork souvlaki, moussaka, pastitsio or a tomato braise: the most food-friendly Greek red on a list.

Agiorgitiko from the slopes aged under the national Reserve term: vanilla, cedar, dried fig and tobacco over the plum, firmer and darker, a wine for roast meat and aged cheese and the style the best estates stake their names on.

Four years at least between oak and bottle, from old vines on the slopes: dried fruit, leather, spice and a long, warm finish, the Peloponnese's answer to Naoussa's Grande Reserve with softer tannin and more flesh.

The old style of the valley floor, rare on the market: Agiorgitiko dried in the sun or picked overripe, naturally sweet or fortified, giving raisin, fig, chocolate and spice, the wine behind the old name blood of Hercules. Serve cool with dried fruit, nuts or a chocolate dessert.
Pale to mid pink, strawberry and cherry, soft and easy, from short skin contact; sold as PGI Peloponnese or PGI Corinth because the appellation is red only. Cold, with meze and grilled fish.

The regional blends that made several Nemea houses famous: Cabernet's structure and blackcurrant stiffening Agiorgitiko's plum and spice, aged in French oak, sold as PGI Peloponnese. Decant and serve with lamb or beef.

exam: The three grapes in equal shares: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto; the only three-grape Xinomavro appellation and the only one outside Macedonia.
The place: Thessaly, Larissa, the slopes of Olympus, the Vale of Tempe, the Aegean close by.
The soil phrase: iron-rich weathered schist.
The history: the 1971 decree, decline, revival from the 1990s by a large Macedonian house, the estates since.
The style against Naoussa: fuller, warmer, rounder, deeper in colour, with earth and herbs.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.styles: A third of the blend by rule: the acid, the tannin and the dried-rose and tomato perfume, ripening a little riper on these warm schist terraces than in Macedonia.

grapes.name: Krassato
grapes.styles: A local red, a third of the blend, that brings alcohol, body and roundness to Xinomavro's frame; it is grown almost nowhere else.

grapes.name: Stavroto
grapes.styles: The third grape, also local, adding colour and a softer, fleshier tannin; like Krassato it is barely seen outside Rapsani.

law.classification: Rapsani is a protected designation of origin from the first Greek decrees of 1971, for dry red wine from a delimited zone of terraces around the village of Rapsani on the slopes of Olympus in the Larissa regional unit of Thessaly. The blend is fixed: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto in equal parts, which makes it the only one of the four Xinomavro appellations with three grapes and the only one outside Macedonia. The national Reserve and Grande Reserve ageing terms apply. The appellation ranks no vineyard, and the estates' other wines are PGI Thessaly.
labels: the three grapes, in equal shares by rule
the mountain, often printed as the wine's address
tiers: Rapsani PDO
Dry red from Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto in equal shares, grown on the terraces of Olympus around Rapsani in Thessaly.
Rapsani Reserve
The national Reserve term for PDO reds, Epilegmenos: extended ageing in oak and bottle before release.
Rapsani Grande Reserve
The national Grande Reserve term, Eidika Epilegmenos: four years' ageing at least, divided between oak and bottle.
PGI Thessaly
The regional wine of the whole of Thessaly, for the estates' varietals and blends outside the appellation.

made.viticulture: The old vineyards of Rapsani were field blends: the three grapes planted together as bush vines on dry-stone terraces, picked together and fermented together, which is where the equal-parts rule came from. Many of those terraces were abandoned in the middle of the twentieth century as the village emptied, and the revival of the 1990s replanted on wires in cordon and Guyot, often with each variety in its own block so it can be picked at its own moment. The schist is thin and poor, so vigour is low and yields are small without much effort; the summer hazard is drought, met with careful canopy management on the old terraces, and the sea breeze helps the bunches through August. Harvest runs through September into early October, by hand, with Xinomavro the last to come in.
made.winemaking: Each grape plays a part. Xinomavro gives acid and tannin, Krassato alcohol and body, Stavroto colour and softness, and the appellation asks for them in equal shares, so the winemaker either ferments a field blend together or vinifies three lots and assembles them. Maceration runs two to three weeks in steel or open vats, malolactic follows, and the wine goes to oak, French barriques for the estates and larger casks for the traditional style, for a year in the ordinary wine and for the national minimums in Reserve and Grande Reserve. The reviving house built the appellation's modern name on a Reserve and a Grande Reserve, and the newer estates make brighter, less oaked versions that show the schist. There is no white, rosé or sweet Rapsani; everything else goes out as PGI Thessaly.

places.name: Mount Olympus
places.note: Greece's highest mountain, 2,917 metres at its summit, the home of the ancient gods; the appellation lies on its eastern and south-eastern foot, far below the snow, where the schist terraces catch the sun and the sea air.

places.name: Rapsani
places.note: The village that names the appellation, on the lower slopes above the Vale of Tempe, once a prosperous wine village that emptied in the twentieth century and was replanted from the 1990s.

places.name: The Vale of Tempe
places.note: The gorge of the Pinios between Olympus and Ossa, the ancient road from Macedonia into Thessaly, just south of the vineyards; the river and the sea beyond it cool the lower terraces.

places.name: Mount Ossa and Ambelakia
places.note: Across the Vale, Ossa faces Olympus, and the village of Ambelakia on its slope, little vineyards in Greek, grew rich on red dye rather than wine; a name to keep apart from Rapsani.

producers.name: Tsantali
producers.why: The large Macedonian house that revived Rapsani in the 1990s, replanting the terraces and making the Reserve and Grande Reserve the appellation's calling cards for a generation.

producers.name: Dougos
producers.why: A family estate at Rapsani whose Rapsani and whose varietal wines from the same slopes put a grower's name beside the large house on the Olympus terraces.

producers.name: Thymiopoulos Vineyards
producers.why: The Naoussa estate's Rapsani Terra Petra, from the three grapes on the schist, is the bottle most Advanced candidates taste for the appellation.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean with the mountain's correction: hot, dry summers on the lower terraces, cooler air and later ripening higher up, and the Aegean a few kilometres to the east sending breezes up the slope in the afternoon. Olympus shelters the vineyards from the north-west and gathers cloud on its summit while the terraces stay in sun. Rain falls mostly in winter; drought on the thin schist is the summer hazard and a wet harvest the autumn one.
terroir.soils: Weathered schist and slate, stony, thin and poor, stained red with iron, with pockets of sandstone and gravel: a soil that drains instantly, limits vigour and gives the wine its earthy, mineral stamp. Iron-rich weathered schist is the phrase to attach to Rapsani in an exam.
terroir.topography: Terraced vineyards on the eastern and south-eastern foot of Olympus, Greece's highest mountain at 2,917 metres, climbing from the village of Rapsani and the edge of the Vale of Tempe up the lower slopes; altitude and the mix of schist and aspect vary from terrace to terrace, so the three grapes were traditionally planted together and picked as the site allowed.
terroir.water: The Pinios river cuts the Vale of Tempe between Olympus and Mount Ossa just south of the vineyards on its way to the Aegean, and the sea itself lies close enough to be seen from the upper terraces; both temper the heat of the Thessalian summer.

traps: Rapsani is in Thessaly, not Macedonia; it is the one Xinomavro appellation south of the Macedonian border, and Olympus is its mountain, not Vermio.
Three grapes, not one: a 100% Xinomavro from these slopes cannot be Rapsani.
Krassato and Stavroto are Rapsani's partners; Negoska is Goumenissa's. Do not swap them in a blend question.
Ambelakia, across the Vale of Tempe on Ossa, means little vineyards and is a dye town, not a wine appellation.
Olympus the mountain is in Thessaly and Macedonia; Olympia, the sanctuary of the games, is in the western Peloponnese, nowhere near Rapsani.

wines.note: Medium ruby, deeper than Naoussa, with sour cherry, raspberry, dried tomato, thyme and sweet spice over an earthy, iron-tinged base; medium-plus acid, rounded tannin and a warmer, fuller frame. Serve at 16 to 17 degrees with roast lamb with herbs, grilled sausages, aubergine dishes or a hard cheese.
The blend aged under the national Reserve term: tobacco, leather and dried fig join the fruit, and the schist's earthiness comes forward. The style the reviving house made famous in the 1990s.
Four years at least between cask and bottle; dried flowers, tar and dried tomato on a mellow frame, Rapsani's answer to old Naoussa and a bottle for slow-roasted meat.
The regional wines of the estates: varietal Xinomavro, Limniona and international grapes from Thessaly's vineyards, sold outside the appellation.

exam: Samos: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Moschato Aspro, the only grape.
The styles: Vin Doux fortified early, Vin Doux Naturel and Grand Cru fortified later, Nectar unfortified from sun-dried grapes.
The place: the eastern Aegean, barely two kilometres off Turkey; terraces on Mount Ampelos to about 800 metres.
The union of cooperatives, founded in 1934, and its long hold on the island's wine.
Service: chilled, with fruit and nut desserts and blue cheese; Nectar with caramel and chocolate.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moschato Aspro, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, the only grape of the appellation: orange blossom, apricot, honey and grapey perfume, made fortified or from sun-dried grapes, young and fresh or long-aged and amber.

law.classification: Samos is one of Greece's oldest protected designations of origin, for sweet wine from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains grown on the island. Its categories carry the French terms the trade adopted for its export market: Vin Doux, fortified at or near the start of fermentation; Vin Doux Naturel, fortified after a partial fermentation, with Grand Cru for selected fruit of the best, higher vineyards; and Vin Naturellement Doux, the unfortified sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, sold as Nectar. The old OPE seal for sweet appellation wines covered it. The Union of Winemaking Cooperatives of Samos, founded in 1934, has long made most of the island's wine and owns its best-known labels.
labels: on Samos, the Vin Doux Naturel from selected higher vineyards, not a classified site
the unfortified sun-dried style, legally a vin naturellement doux
tiers: Samos Vin Doux
Fortified at or near the start of fermentation, about 15% alcohol, very sweet and fresh: the island's classic.
Samos Vin Doux Naturel and Grand Cru
Fortified after a partial fermentation; Grand Cru from selected fruit of the best, higher vineyards.
Samos Vin Naturellement Doux (Nectar)
Unfortified, from sun-dried Muscat, fermented to a natural stop and aged in oak.

made.viticulture: The vineyard is a work of stone: narrow terraces, the pezoules, built up the mountain over centuries, too steep and too small for machines, so everything is done by hand. Vines are mostly low bush vines, with newer plantings on wires on the gentler ground. Muscat Blanc is thin-skinned, prone to rot and to sunburn, and its compact bunches suffer in a wet autumn, so the higher, airier terraces are prized. Yields are low on the mountain and higher on the plain. Because the terraces climb from the coast to about 800 metres, the harvest runs for weeks, from the lowest vines in late summer to the highest in autumn, and the growers deliver their grapes to the union's wineries. Picking date sets the style: ripe fruit for the Vin Doux, the best fruit of the high terraces for the Grand Cru, and overripe fruit laid out in the sun for Nectar. The labour of the terraces, and the loss of growers to other work, is the vineyard's lasting threat.
made.winemaking: Samos makes sweet wine in three ways. For the Vin Doux, grape spirit is added to the must at or just after the start of fermentation, keeping almost all of the grape's sugar and raising the alcohol to about 15 per cent. For the Vin Doux Naturel and the Grand Cru, the must ferments partway before the spirit stops it, which gives a little more complexity. For Nectar, the Muscat is dried in the sun for days until the grapes shrivel, then fermented slowly without any spirit to a natural stop and aged in oak for several years. The young fortified wines are kept in tank for freshness; the long-aged wines, such as Anthemis, spend years in oak and turn amber. A small amount of Muscat is fermented dry for the modern dry white.

places.name: Mount Ampelos
places.note: The central massif whose name means vine, terraced on its northern and central slopes up to about 800 metres: the heart of Samos Muscat and the source of its Grand Cru fruit.

places.name: Vourliotes
places.note: A mountain village on the northern slopes above the coast, amid some of the island's highest and most admired terraces.

places.name: Manolates
places.note: A village high on the northern side of Ampelos, whose terraces are among the coolest and latest to be picked.

places.name: Karlovasi and the west
places.note: The island's second town and port in the west, with vineyards on the lower slopes towards Mount Kerkis and on the coastal ground, where riper, earlier fruit grows.

places.name: Vathy
places.note: The capital and port on a deep bay in the north-east, the harbour from which the island's wine has long been shipped.

places.name: Mount Kerkis
places.note: The higher, rockier mountain in the west, over 1,400 metres, whose slopes carry fewer vines but shelter the western vineyards.

producers.name: Union of Winemaking Cooperatives of Samos (Samos Wines)
producers.why: Founded in 1934, the growers' union that makes most of the island's wine: the Vin Doux, the Grand Cru, Nectar, the long-aged Anthemis and a dry Muscat, the labels any server meets.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean, hot and dry in summer and mild and wet in winter, but greener than most Aegean islands because its mountains catch the rain. The north side, facing the sea and the summer northerlies, is cooler and moister; the south is hotter. Altitude matters most: the terraces climb from near sea level to about 800 metres, and the harvest is staggered over many weeks, from late summer on the coast to autumn high on the mountain, giving a wide range of ripeness on one small island.
terroir.soils: Poor, stony and well drained: schist across much of the mountain, with limestone, clay and sandy patches, all held in place by stone-walled terraces. The thin soils limit vigour and yield and concentrate the Muscat's perfume; the deeper ground near the coast gives larger crops and simpler wine.
terroir.topography: A mountainous island with two main massifs: Mount Ampelos, whose name means vine, in the centre and north, and the higher Mount Kerkis in the west, over 1,400 metres. The vineyards climb the northern and central slopes of Ampelos in narrow terraces, around villages such as Vourliotes and Manolates, and spread across the lower ground near Karlovasi in the west. The capital, Vathy, lies on a deep bay in the north-east.
terroir.water: The Aegean surrounds the island, and the narrow Mycale strait separates it from Turkey. Mountain streams and springs make the north of Samos unusually green, and sea breezes and altitude cool the terraces through the hot summer.

traps: Samos Vin Doux is fortified; Samos Nectar is not, it is made from sun-dried grapes, like Santorini's Vinsanto.
Grand Cru on Samos is a style from selected higher vineyards, not a classified vineyard as in Burgundy or Alsace.
Samos uses Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains; the Muscat of Lemnos is Muscat of Alexandria.
Samos is in the eastern Aegean near Turkey, not in the Cyclades with Santorini.
The French terms on the label are the appellation's own categories for an export wine, not a sign that the wine is French.

wines.note: The everyday classic: grape spirit added to the must at or near the start of fermentation, to about 15 per cent alcohol, very sweet and fresh, golden, with orange blossom, apricot and honey. Serve chilled with fruit tarts, baklava or cheese.

A Vin Doux Naturel from selected fruit of the best, higher vineyards, fermented partway and then fortified: more complex than the Vin Doux, with apricot, citrus peel, honey and spice and a cleaner, longer finish. Serve with blue cheese, foie gras or almond desserts.

Unfortified sweet wine from sun-dried Muscat, fermented to a natural stop and aged for several years in oak: amber, dried apricot, fig, raisin, caramel and spice, rich yet fresh. Serve with crème brûlée, bread pudding, nuts or chocolate.
Long cask-aged versions, the union's Anthemis the best known: amber, orange marmalade, toffee and nuts, a Greek cousin to an aged Muscat de Rivesaltes or a Rutherglen Muscat.
A modern sideline: Muscat fermented dry, floral and grapey with a bitter orange finish, a striking aperitif with meze and a lesson that Muscat smells sweet without being sweet.

exam: Assyrtiko: at least 85% of dry Santorini, with Athiri and Aidani; at least 51% of Vinsanto.
The vineyard: own-rooted vines in volcanic ash and pumice, no phylloxera because there is no clay, kouloura baskets against the meltemi.
Water: almost no summer rain; night humidity and dew soaked up by the pumice.
The three wines: dry Santorini, Nykteri with oak, and Vinsanto from sun-dried grapes aged at least two years in cask.
The place: southern Cyclades, north of Crete; a caldera left by the Bronze Age eruption that buried Akrotiri.
The glass: bone dry, high acid, saline and flinty, with alcohol and weight; one of the great ageing whites of a hot climate.
An appellation since 1971 and white only; Mavrotragano and other reds are PGI Cyclades.

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.styles: At least 85% of dry Santorini and 51% of Vinsanto: lemon, lime, flint, salt and smoke, piercing acid with real alcohol and weight, the rare white that keeps its acidity in a hot, dry climate.

grapes.name: Athiri
grapes.styles: A soft, lemony, low-acid white that may make up part of the remainder of a dry Santorini, adding perfume and roundness.

grapes.name: Aidani
grapes.styles: An aromatic white of flowers and herbs, the main partner of Assyrtiko in Vinsanto and a permitted minor share of the dry wine.

grapes.name: Mavrotragano
grapes.styles: A revived, nearly lost red of the island, deep, firm and spicy, made into serious dry red sold as PGI Cyclades.

grapes.name: Mandilaria
grapes.styles: A deeply coloured, tannic red grown on the island for reds and rosés sold as PGI Cyclades, since the appellation is white.

law.classification: Santorini was among the first Greek appellations, decreed in 1971, and is a protected designation of origin for wine from the island's own vineyards. The dry white must contain at least 85% Assyrtiko, the remainder Athiri and Aidani; older guides give 75%, the rule before an amendment of recent years. Nykteri is a protected term within the appellation for a riper dry white with at least 13.5% alcohol and at least three months in oak. Vinsanto is the sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, at least 51% Assyrtiko with Aidani the main partner, aged at least two years in oak. The appellation is white; reds, rosés and dry wines outside these rules are sold as PGI Cyclades.
labels: of the night: the riper, oak-aged dry white
the sun-dried sweet wine of Santorini, written as one word
a traditional Santorini winery, often dug into the pumice
tiers: Santorini PDO dry white
At least 85% Assyrtiko with Athiri and Aidani, from the island's own-rooted vines; oaked or unoaked, the wine every exam means by Santorini.
Nykteri
A protected term of the appellation: dry Santorini from riper grapes, at least 13.5% alcohol and at least three months in oak.
Vinsanto
The sweet wine of sun-dried grapes, at least 51% Assyrtiko with Aidani, aged at least two years in cask; one word, and never fortified.
PGI Cyclades
The regional wine of the island group: Mavrotragano and Mandilaria reds, rosés and whites outside the appellation's rules.

made.viticulture: Santorini's vines are among the oldest living vineyards in Europe. Because phylloxera cannot survive in the ash, the vines grow on their own roots, and when a vine tires the grower cuts it back or layers it and lets the old root system throw new wood, so a root may be centuries old while the visible vine is young. The classic training is the kouloura: the canes are woven year after year into a low basket lying on the ground, with the grapes hanging inside, sheltered from the meltemi, from blown sand and from the sun. Some vines are kept as low bush vines, and a few modern plots are on wires. There is no irrigation; plantings are sparse to share the little water, and yields are tiny, a fraction of a mainland vineyard's. Harvest is by hand, often on the knees, usually in August, among the first in Greece. The threats are drought, wind and the pull of tourism on land and labour.
made.winemaking: Dry Santorini is made mostly in a protective style: grapes picked in the early morning, pressed, settled and fermented cool in stainless steel, often with some lees ageing and without malolactic conversion, so the wine keeps its acid and salt. A growing number of producers use native yeasts, older oak or long lees contact for texture. Nykteri takes its name from night work, when grapes were picked and pressed before dawn to escape the heat; today it is a riper wine with at least 13.5 per cent alcohol and at least three months in oak. Vinsanto is made from late-picked grapes laid out in the sun for a week or two until they shrivel, pressed to a thick must that ferments slowly to low alcohol and very high sugar, then aged at least two years in old casks, often far longer. The name is usually traced to the wine of Santorini traded through Venice, and in the nineteenth century much of it went to Russia for the Orthodox communion.

places.name: Pyrgos and the centre
places.note: The heart of the vineyard in the middle of the island, around Pyrgos, the highest village, below Profitis Ilias, with Megalochori, Episkopi Gonia and Exo Gonia on the slopes and plains around it.

places.name: Pyrgos
places.note: The highest village of Santorini, under the limestone peak of Profitis Ilias, with some of the coolest, windiest vineyards on the island and an old tradition of Vinsanto.

places.name: Megalochori
places.note: A village south-west of Pyrgos with old vineyards towards the caldera and several historic and modern wineries.

places.name: Episkopi Gonia
places.note: A village on the eastern plain below Pyrgos, home of old family estates and very old basket-trained vines.

places.name: Exo Gonia
places.note: A village on the slope between Pyrgos and the eastern coast, with vineyards falling towards the sea and several modern wineries.

places.name: The north
places.note: The narrowing arm of the crescent from Fira and Imerovigli on the caldera's edge to Oia at the tip, windswept and dry, with vineyards on the gentler outer slope and the sandy flats.

places.name: Oia
places.note: The village at the northern tip of the island, with vineyards on its exposed slopes and flats and one of the island's most celebrated estates.

places.name: Fira and Imerovigli
places.note: The island's capital and its neighbour on the caldera's rim, with vineyards behind them on the plain falling east towards the sea.

places.name: Akrotiri and the south
places.note: The southern arm of the crescent, around the buried Bronze Age town of Akrotiri and the village of Emporio, flatter and hotter, with wide vineyards of old baskets.

places.name: Akrotiri
places.note: The south-western peninsula and its village, whose name the excavated Bronze Age town under the ash now carries, with exposed vineyards facing the wind and the caldera.

places.name: Emporio
places.note: The largest village of the south, on the plain below Profitis Ilias, surrounded by old basket-trained vineyards.

places.name: Thirasia
places.note: The smaller island on the western side of the caldera, a fragment of the old volcano's rim, with a few basket-trained vineyards of its own on the same ash.

places.name: Profitis Ilias
places.note: The island's highest point, at about 570 metres, a block of older limestone that the volcano built around; it shelters the vineyards of Pyrgos and Exo Gonia.

producers.name: Domaine Sigalas
producers.why: An estate at Oia in the north, founded in 1991, whose Santorini and single-vineyard Kavalieros set a modern standard for site-driven Assyrtiko.

producers.name: Estate Argyros
producers.why: A family estate at Episkopi Gonia, founded in 1903, with some of the island's oldest own-rooted vines; its Cuvée Monsignori and long-aged Vinsanto are benchmarks.

producers.name: Gaia Wines
producers.why: Founded in 1994, with a Santorini winery whose Thalassitis showed the world sharp, saline Assyrtiko and whose native-yeast wines followed; also a leading Nemea house.

producers.name: Hatzidakis
producers.why: A small organic estate at Pyrgos, known for powerful old-vine Assyrtiko, Nykteri and Mavrotragano from a cellar cut into the pumice.

producers.name: Gavalas
producers.why: One of the island's old family wineries, at Megalochori, keeping traditional Nykteri, Vinsanto and rare local grapes alive.

producers.name: Santo Wines
producers.why: The union of the island's growers' cooperatives, founded in 1947, which takes the grapes of many smallholders and makes the full range from dry Assyrtiko to Vinsanto.

producers.name: Boutari
producers.why: The Naoussa house, among the first mainland producers to build a modern winery on the island, at Megalochori.

terroir.climate: Hot, arid Mediterranean, with a few hundred millimetres of rain a year, almost all of it in winter, and long cloudless summers. Two forces make vines possible. The meltemi, the strong northerly wind of July and August, cools the island but batters and dries any exposed shoot. The humidity off the sea at night settles as dew and is soaked up by the porous pumice, feeding the roots through the drought. Fungal disease is rare in the dry, windy air, and the harvest comes early, usually in August.
terroir.soils: Volcanic through and through: layers of ash, pumice and lava from the island's eruptions, the greatest of them in the Late Bronze Age, which buried the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri. The local soil, called aspa, is sandy, porous and very poor, with almost no organic matter and no clay, so phylloxera, which needs clay to survive and spread, cannot live in it. The pumice holds the night's moisture like a sponge, and the volcanic rock is part of the wine's salt and stone.
terroir.topography: What remains of a volcano whose centre collapsed into the sea: a crescent of land, with Thirasia and Aspronisi completing the ring and the young volcanic islets of Nea and Palea Kameni in the middle of the flooded caldera. The cliffs on the inner side drop hundreds of metres to the water; the outer side slopes gently east and south to black sand beaches, and that slope is where most vines grow. The highest vineyards lie around Pyrgos, under Profitis Ilias, the island's one real mountain, a block of older limestone.
terroir.water: No rivers, no springs worth the name and almost no rain in the growing season: the sea is the island's only water, arriving as wind-borne humidity and night dew. The meltemi off the Aegean is the sea's other gift, cooling the vines and keeping disease away, at the price of salty, damaging gusts.

traps: Vinsanto, one word, is Santorini's; Vin Santo, two words, is Tuscany's; neither is fortified.
Older guides give 75% Assyrtiko for dry Santorini; the current rule is at least 85%.
The kouloura protects against wind, sand and sun; it is not a defence against phylloxera, which the ash keeps away by itself.
Nykteri means of the night, from the old night picking and pressing; today it means riper and oak-aged, not harvested after dark.
Vinsanto is made from white grapes, though it ages to a deep amber, almost red-brown colour; it is not a red wine.
Assyrtiko grows on the mainland and on other islands too; only wine from the Santorini group itself may carry the name Santorini.

wines.note: Pale lemon with a green glint: lemon, lime, flint, smoke and sea salt, bone dry with searing acid, real body and 13 to 14.5 per cent alcohol. It opens over hours and ages for ten years and more towards honey and toast. Serve at 8 to 10 degrees with oysters, grilled fish, crab, shrimp and anything dressed with lemon and olive oil.

The traditional night-pressed wine, today a riper Santorini aged at least three months in oak: fuller and rounder, with toast and dried citrus over the salt. Serve a touch warmer with richer fish, lobster or roast poultry.

Assyrtiko and Aidani dried in the sun and aged at least two years in cask: amber to mahogany, with dried apricot, fig, raisin, coffee and orange peel, very sweet yet lifted by Assyrtiko's acid. Serve cool with blue cheese, nut tarts or chocolate, or on its own.

Single-vineyard and old-vine bottlings, some fermented with native yeast or aged on lees or in oak, all sold as Santorini: deeper in texture, with the same salt and acid, and the most age-worthy dry whites of the island.
Dry red from the revived local grape, sold as PGI Cyclades: deep colour, black fruit, spice and firm tannin with the island's freshness; a rarity and a fine talking point at the table.
